newsitem.title: FRANCE: French National Front mayor tried for racist slur.
newsitem.headline: French National Front mayor tried for racist slur.

text.p: A French state prosecutor on Monday asked a court to ban from public office National Front town mayor Catherine Megret, who is charged with making racist insults in a newspaper interview.

Three anti-racism associations and more than 700 private citizens took the far-right mayor of Vitrolles in southern France to court for inciting racial hatred and discrimination in the interview with the German daily Berliner Zeitung.
In the recorded interview, given shortly after she was elected last February, she called immigrants "colonialists" and espoused racial inequality.
The prosecutor did not say for how long Megret should be declared ineligible for public office, and asked the court to fine her an unspecified amount. The verdict was expected at a later date.

Foes of the National Front booed as Megret, accompanied by her husband Bruno Megret, the anti-immigrant party's number two, and the National Front mayor of Toulon, Jean-Marie le Chevallier left the heavily guarded the Aix-en-Provence law courts.
Bruno Megret went on to tell a rally of Front supporters the trial was a witch hunt and an infringement of freedom of speech.
Catherine Megret captured a fourth French town for the Front in a by-election after her husband was disqualified from running because he exceeded the legal ceiling on campaign expenses.
The trial coincided with soul-searching in the mainstream French right, defeated by the left in June 1 parliamentary elections, about relations with the National Front.

The Front, which advocates sending immigrants home, has been held at arm's length by mainstream parties, but the right has begun wondering aloud how to re-capture the Front's 15 percent share of voters.
French media on Monday played up confirmation by Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen and right-wing Gaullist Robert Pandraud they they dined together at a Paris restaurant last week.
Pandraud, a former cabinet minister, said that neither the Front nor President Jacques Chirac's Gaullist RPR parties wanted to strike an alliance at the moment, but he favoured a dialogue.
Asked if the RPR should start talks with the Front, the RPR Secretary General Jean-Louis Debre told the conservative newspaper Le Figaro in an interview published on Monday:
"It is important for the movement's leaders to debate the issue in the coming months and agree on a clear position."

Debre, the former interior minister, said Gaullists would fight those who did not have the same ideas. But he appeared to be softer to the Front than to the left, saying: "Socialism is bad for France. The Front defends values which are not those of Gaullism."
